method_laws: A branch defined on a COUNT cannot answer a MEMBERSHIP question. F_SMALL_FAMILY fired correctly at 5 survivors and the verdict prose then claimed the actor was one of them -- an assumption the measurement never made. Put the actor's membership INSIDE the branch definition whenever the card asks whether a specific unit is special.

A permutation p-value's draw count has TWO separate consequences, and they bind on different objects: the RESOLUTION FLOOR 1/(B+1) decides whether the FAMILY's strongest members can be rejected at all (at B=2000 nothing could be, and 2 of 3 substrates' survivors sit AT the floor), while the tail probability's confidence interval decides whether a PARTICULAR unit can ever clear its own BH requirement. Compute both before calling a non-survival a power problem.

An UNCORRECTED percentile on a preselected unit and a multiplicity-corrected one can disagree by an order of magnitude (.0145 -> q .157 = 10.8x) while the underlying measurement is bit-identical. The correction is not a detail of presentation; it is the difference between a claim and a description.

When a card's own framing predicts the uncomfortable answer (Kriegeskorte's policy step (1) predicts the actor may be one of many), scoring the registered prediction FALSE is the cheap part; the work is deriving what the prior claim becomes, which is a different sentence, not a weaker adverb.
limitations: The addendum is POST-HOC: nothing here carries a registered branch.
BH assumes p-values are valid; permutation p-values here are censored at 5.00e-05 and discrete, so q-values near the floor are conservative.
The Wilson interval is a normal-score approximation; the exact Clopper-Pearson interval would be marginally wider and is not computed (no new dependency introduced).
Survivor-family membership is read on three non-independent substrates of ONE specimen; 'transport' here means substrate robustness, never cross-specimen replication.
DNp33's type median remains a 2-POINT statistic (L213 limit 1).
